opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the most important forces shaping the world right now, alongside debt, internal conflict, international great-power conflict, and acts of nature. And of those, technology, and AI in particular, is probably the one that's going to change things the most, because it changes how we think.

The way I look at it is through a lot of history. Throughout time, human inventiveness has been the thing that raised productivity, and productivity is what raises living standards. When you look at the printing press, the steam engine, electricity, the computer, each one extended human capability. But this one is different in an important way, because it doesn't just extend our muscles or our memory. It extends our thinking. It's going to be like having an enormous number of very smart people available to you, essentially for free.

I've been doing this for a long time. Back in the early 1980s I started writing down my decision-making criteria and putting them into algorithms, so that the computer and I could think together. It was like playing chess with a partner, where I could see the computer's reasoning and it could process far more than I could. So I've lived with this idea of human and machine thinking in partnership for over forty years. What's changed is the magnitude. These systems now can do so much of what we used to consider uniquely human thinking.

So what does that mean for human capabilities? A few things. First, the people who learn to use it well are going to be enormously more capable than those who don't. It's going to create a big gap. Second, a lot of jobs are going to be displaced, and that's going to raise big questions about wealth gaps and opportunity gaps, which are already a source of internal conflict. Third, whoever leads in this technology is going to have a big advantage both economically and militarily, which is why it's at the center of the conflict between the United States and China.

But I want to be careful about one thing. There's a difference between what the machine can do and what we should let it decide. I would never let a machine make a decision when I don't understand the reasoning behind it. These large language models are great at giving you an answer, but they don't necessarily understand cause and effect the way a well-thought-out decision system does. So you have to use it as a partner and keep your own judgment.

And then there's the deeper question: what makes us human? I think it's going to push us toward the things that machines can't replace, which is relationships, meaning, purpose, how we treat each other. Ultimately, it's not about what the technology can do. It's about how we use it. If we use it well, it can be one of the greatest periods of prosperity in history. If we use it badly, combined with the other forces I mentioned, it could be very dangerous. So I'd say to people: learn it, engage with it, but don't give up your own independent thinking.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts earlier technologies that extended muscles or memory with AI, which extends thinking and can do much of what was considered uniquely human thinking.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think about it the way I think about everything, which is to look at how these things have happened over history, because it's not really new. I mean, the specifics are new, but the pattern isn't. Every big technological revolution—the printing press, the industrial revolution, computers—took something that humans did and made it radically cheaper and more scalable, and then it changed who had power and how people lived. So the first thing I'd say is, don't look at this as a unique event. Look at it as the latest and probably the most powerful version of something that has happened many times before.

Now, what's different about this one is that the previous revolutions mostly amplified our physical capabilities or our ability to move information around. This one is amplifying thinking itself. And I've lived this. At Bridgewater, going back to the early eighties, I started writing down my criteria for making decisions—literally, when I made a decision, I'd write down the reasoning—and then we'd turn those into algorithms and have the computer make the decisions alongside me. And what I found was that the computer and I together were much better than either one alone. The computer could process far more than I could, it had no emotion, it didn't get greedy or fearful. But I could see things that it couldn't see, because it only knew what it had been given. So that partnership—that's what I think the real change is. Not man versus machine. It's the quality of the partnership.

And that leads to the important question, which is: what is it that we as humans are going to be uniquely good at? Because a lot of what we think of as intelligence—remembering things, calculating, even a lot of reasoning—is going to be done better by the machines. So what's left is things like judgment, wisdom, knowing what questions to ask, understanding what matters and what doesn't. And frankly, the ability to get along with each other, which may turn out to be the most important thing of all.

But I'd also say this, and it's the part people don't like to hear. Technology doesn't determine whether the outcome is good or bad. People do. The same printing press that spread knowledge also spread propaganda and helped produce a hundred years of religious wars. So the question of whether AI raises human capability or whether it's used in a way that's destructive—that's going to depend on how we deal with each other, internally within countries and between countries. And right now, if I look at the five big forces I watch—the debt cycle, the internal political conflict, the international conflict, acts of nature, and technology—technology is the one that's most positive, but it's happening in an environment where the other four are very stressed. And that worries me. Because the greatest capability in the hands of people who are fighting with each other is not necessarily a good thing.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts earlier technological revolutions that amplified physical capabilities or information handling with AI, which amplifies thinking itself.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish between intelligence and judgment. Artificial intelligence will expand our ability to process information, identify patterns, and explore possibilities. Things that once required a great deal of expertise will become accessible to many more people.

But having an answer isn’t the same as knowing whether it’s a good answer. You still have to ask: What assumptions went into this? Where could it be wrong? And what am I trying to accomplish?

In investing, you learn that a model can work beautifully until circumstances change in a way it hasn’t accounted for. So the powerful combination is a person who understands how to question the machine, working with a machine that helps them question their own thinking.

The technological capability is only part of the story. How those benefits are distributed, how people adapt, and how we give people meaningful roles—those will be enormous challenges.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses AI expanding information processing and pattern recognition, but does not describe replacement progressing from bodily functions to aspects of the mind.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of AI as a tremendous expansion of our ability to think. We’ve built machines that extend our muscles, and now we’re building machines that extend our minds. They can process information, find patterns, and help us make decisions on a scale that an individual couldn’t.

But you still have to ask: What are you trying to accomplish, and how do you know whether the answer is good? If you accept an answer without understanding its limitations, you can make mistakes much faster, too.

So I think the important capability will be knowing how to work with that intelligence—how to ask good questions, test the answers, and exercise judgment. And then there’s a separate question: How do we manage the consequences for people whose work changes? Greater capability creates enormous opportunity, but how we handle it matters.

r001.rationale: The response describes machines extending human muscles and then human minds, clearly framing AI’s capability expansion as moving from bodily to mental functions.
